activities.anchor: Two photographers stand at the same market stall at noon
activities.caption: bet before you read on — why are both pictures equally bright?
activities.name: expDuoPredict

config.q: One photographer shoots f/1.8, the other f/16 — yet both portraits come out exactly the same brightness. What explains it?
choices: The camera's meter quietly corrected the second shot
A 'correct' exposure can be made a thousand different ways — each dial trades light for a side effect
f/16 actually gathers the same light as f/1.8 at the same shutter speed
One of the two photographs is secretly misexposed
config.why: Each dial controls the light AND something else — aperture depth of field, shutter motion, ISO noise. Same bucket level, entirely different photographs; neither is 'more correct'.

activities.anchor: three dials that each control the light
activities.caption: file each job under the dial that does it
activities.name: expDialSort

config.prompt: Three dials, each doing double duty — file each job:

items.label: depth of field — how much of the scene melts
the tap's width in the bucket analogy
motion — freeze the wingbeat or streak it

config.why: The side effects are the photograph's central creative decision — the bookkeeping only tells you what each choice costs.

activities.anchor: the lens's focal length divided by
activities.caption: place the marker two stops wider than f/8
activities.name: expStopPlace

config.prompt: Two stops wider than f/8 — place the marker on the standard f-number scale:
config.why: Each full stop up the scale halves the light: f/8 → f/5.6 is one stop, f/5.6 → f/4 is two — and remember the scale runs backwards, so wider opening = smaller number.

activities.caption: rebuild the Sunny 16 portrait exchange, step by step
activities.name: expSunnyOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the exchange that melts a Sunny 16 landscape into a portrait:
items: Sunny 16 baseline: bright daylight gives f/16 at 1/125 s with ISO 100 — no meter needed
A portrait wants the background melted, so open to f/2.8 — four stops wider (f/16 → f/11 → f/8 → f/5.6 → f/4 → f/2.8)
Pay it back on the shutter — four stops faster
1/125 → 1/250 → 1/500 → 1/1000 → 1/2000 s: same bucket level, razor-thin focus and a dissolved background
config.why: The stop is the universal currency: give one dial four stops, pay it back on another — the exchange cashed the same light for different side effects.

activities.caption: pair each depth-of-field lever with its pull
activities.name: expDofMatch

config.prompt: Depth of field answers to four levers — pair each with what it does:

pairs.right: shallower focus — light cones from out-of-focus points are wider and blur faster
shallows the focus at the same aperture and framing
the plane of sharpness falls thinner
invites longer focal lengths for the same framing — full-frame portraits melt backgrounds more readily
maximises the sharp range from foreground to infinity — the landscape trick

config.why: Portraits at f/1.8 isolate a face, landscapes at f/11 hold everything crisp, street shooters pick f/8 to forgive imperfect timing.

activities.caption: drag the divider — blur as failure vs blur as meaning
activities.name: expBlurCompare

config.prompt: One shutter dial, two opposite intents — drag to compare:

before.label: frozen
before.text: 1/250 s handles walking people; 1/500–1/1000 s handles running and most sport; 1/2000 s and beyond freezes birds, water splashes and ball strikes. Handheld, keep the shutter no slower than 1/focal-length seconds unless stabilisation helps.

after.label: deliberately blurred
after.text: Panning a cyclist at 1/30 s keeps the subject sharp while the world streaks — speed made visible. Long exposures turn waterfalls to silk and traffic into light rivers (tripod mandatory; in daylight a neutral-density filter buys the missing stops). Stars run 10–25 seconds before Earth's rotation smears them.

config.why: Blur is a vocabulary, not a mistake — the skill is knowing the freezing speeds well enough that what you keep is what you meant to keep.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's metering notes
activities.name: expMeterSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's metering notes is wrong — click it:
lines: The built-in meter is a reflected-light meter: it reads the light bouncing off the scene.
Its fixed assumption: the scene, on average, reflects middle grey.
Snow photographs come back grey because the meter underexposes the white toward grey — add about +2 stops of compensation.
Evaluative/matrix metering meters a tiny circle — the tool for deliberately placing one tone.
The histogram graphs brightness from left (black) to right (white).
config.correction: That describes spot metering; evaluative/matrix reads the whole frame against a database of scenes, and centre-weighted privileges the middle.
config.why: Metering modes are different opinions operationalised — and the histogram is the feedback loop that reports who was right.

activities.anchor: The meter is an opinion with a fixed assumption
activities.caption: true or false — trusting the meter
activities.name: expGreyJudge

statements.s: The camera's automatic exposure is an objective measurement of the scene.
statements.why: It is an opinion with a fixed assumption — hardware is not what fails on extreme scenes; the assumption is.

statements.s: The meter's instruction is: make what I measure average out to middle grey.
statements.why: Brilliant for average scenes, systematically wrong at the extremes — hence grey snow.

statements.s: A washed-out night shot means the camera is faulty and needs repair.
statements.why: The fix is override, not repair — exposure compensation exists precisely because you know whether this scene should be grey.

statements.s: Pushing ISO to 6400 at a concert is compensating for ignorance.
statements.why: Grain that preserves a moment beats noise-free blur of nothing — ISO is the escape dial, honoured rather than shamed.
